Family Health

Vaginal dryness: causes, assessment and treatment choices

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Vaginal dryness can affect everyday comfort as well as wanted sexual activity. It is common around menopause, but age is not the only explanation and discomfort does not have to be endured. A useful plan identifies the cause and distinguishes products for friction, ongoing moisture and hormone-related tissue changes.

Recognise the pattern without assuming the cause

Lower oestrogen around menopause can leave vaginal tissues thinner, less elastic and more easily irritated, with changes in their usual environment. Dryness, burning, soreness, painful penetration and some urinary symptoms may occur together as genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM. Symptoms can continue without treatment rather than disappearing automatically after the final period.

Dryness can also affect the vulva, the external genital skin, and it may be noticeable without sex. It does not by itself diagnose menopause, infection or a hormone deficiency. New discharge, a skin change or bleeding needs its own assessment; even when fragile tissue could contribute, do not assume that dryness explains blood.

Consider medicines, life stages and other conditions

Oestrogen levels can change after birth, during breastfeeding, after removal of both ovaries or with some cancer treatments and anti-oestrogen medicines. Removing the uterus without both ovaries is a different operation. Hormonal contraception, some antidepressants and certain cold or allergy medicines can also contribute to dryness; the exact drug and timing matter.

Perfumed washes, vaginal douching and irritating products may worsen symptoms without a hormone problem. Sjögren's disease can cause vaginal dryness alongside dry eyes or mouth; diabetes and skin conditions may also be relevant. Not every autoimmune illness works through low oestrogen. Tell the clinician about broader symptoms and all medicines rather than stopping necessary treatment or diagnosing yourself.

What a clinical assessment may involve

Arrange a consultation if dryness affects your life, simple measures have not helped after a few weeks, or symptoms persist or worry you. You can start by saying that the tissues feel dry, sore or uncomfortable. Bring a list of prescription medicines, pharmacy products, supplements and washes; mention periods, pregnancy possibility, breastfeeding, smoking, operations and cancer treatment when relevant.

An examination may help identify tissue changes, irritation, infection or a particular lesion. Ask for an explanation, a chaperone if wanted, a pause or an end at any stage. Tests such as a swab, urine sample or a biopsy are selected for findings, not required for everyone. Cervical screening is not a general infection test or a replacement for investigating symptoms, and a reassuring screening result does not explain persistent bleeding.

Lubricant and moisturiser have different jobs

A purpose-made lubricant reduces friction during sexual activity. A water-based product is a reasonable starting option; reapply or change it if necessary and stop if it irritates. Check condom and toy compatibility, because oil-based products can weaken latex. Lubricant does not diagnose or treat every cause of pain.

A vaginal moisturiser is intended for more regular use for ongoing dryness, whether or not you have sex. Follow the particular product's instructions; no single duration of relief applies to every formulation. Ordinary body lotion, perfumed creams and oral supplements are not substitutes for products intended for vaginal use. A pharmacist can help you choose, and persistent symptoms still need review.

Reduce irritation and keep intimacy voluntary

Keep external washing gentle and avoid internal washing, douches, fragranced sprays and repeated experiments with products that sting. Removing an irritant may help, but extra scrubbing or trying to make the vagina sterile can add soreness. If a product worsens symptoms, stop it and note its name for the consultation.

When you want sexual contact, time for arousal, comfortable touch and lubricant may improve comfort. There is no requirement to have more intercourse to prevent or cure dryness, and lubrication does not replace consent. Stop or change an activity that hurts; choose nonpenetrative intimacy if preferred. Ongoing pain or involuntary tightening deserves assessment rather than pressure to try harder.

Local oestrogen is different from systemic HRT

For menopause-related tissue symptoms, a clinician may offer low-dose vaginal oestrogen as a cream, gel, tablet, pessary or ring. It acts mainly in the local tissues, with much less absorption into the bloodstream than systemic hormone therapy. It can sometimes be used alongside systemic HRT, with moisturiser or lubricant if helpful; it does not treat hot flushes by itself or provide contraception.

The exact product and dose still matter. Low-dose local treatment usually does not require an added progestogen, while systemic oestrogen generally needs womb protection with a progestogen when the uterus is present. Do not transfer advice between every cream, ring, tablet or patch. Tell the prescriber if pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding; if pregnancy is suspected while using vaginal oestrogen, stop it and contact the prescriber.

Discuss side effects and medical history individually

Headache, abdominal or vaginal discomfort, irritation or spotting can occur with local treatment. Nausea, breast tenderness, fluid retention, weight or skin changes depend on the preparation and circumstances; they are not inevitable effects of every vaginal product. Serious effects with low-dose vaginal oestrogen are rare, and a list of systemic HRT risks for clots, stroke or breast and ovarian cancer should not be applied as an identical risk estimate to local therapy. Report unexplained bleeding and persistent or troublesome effects.

A history of breast cancer is a reason for an individual discussion, not a blanket instruction to endure symptoms. Non-hormonal options are usually tried first; persistent symptoms may justify discussion of local oestrogen with appropriate specialists, particularly during aromatase-inhibitor treatment, because recurrence-risk uncertainty remains. Other selected prescription options, such as vaginal prasterone or oral ospemifene, have their own suitability and safety rules. Do not start a hormone or hormone-like supplement yourself.

Soy and herbal products are not assured alternatives

Soy foods can be part of an ordinary varied diet, but eating soy is not a dependable prescription for vaginal dryness. Some phyto-oestrogen studies suggest modest benefits, often with limitations, and food, oral extracts and vaginal research formulations are different. Concentrated supplements need a product and medicine review, especially with a hormone-sensitive cancer history.

Black cohosh has been studied for some menopause symptoms, with findings depending on the product; this does not establish a reliable dryness treatment. Rare liver-injury reports and interactions warrant caution, and the cause of every reported injury is not certain. A small wild-yam cream trial did not show a significant advantage over placebo for menopausal symptoms or hormone levels. Neither herb is a proven replacement for symptom-specific care, and natural does not mean risk-free.

When symptoms need quicker help

Have bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause assessed rather than attributing it to dryness. Any postmenopausal bleeding, even once or a small pink or brown stain, deserves a check. New unusual discharge, sores or persistent urinary symptoms also need review. Seek same-day advice for pelvic pain with fever, unusual discharge, urinary symptoms or possible pregnancy; contact maternity or early-pregnancy care immediately for any bleeding during pregnancy.

Seek immediate emergency assessment for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or loss of consciousness, or breathing difficulty. During treatment, pain, redness or swelling in one leg needs urgent same-day advice; chest pain with breathlessness, stroke-like symptoms or sudden tongue or throat swelling needs emergency care. Do not wait for a moisturiser or hormone product to work.

Agree on follow-up and a measure of improvement

Ask what the treatment is intended to improve, how to use the specific product and when to review it. For menopause treatment, a review at about three months and then annually is usual, with earlier help for side effects, warning signs or insufficient benefit. Local oestrogen may take time to work fully, and symptoms can return after stopping; ongoing care is an individual decision, not a failure.

A short record of dryness, soreness, urinary symptoms and the products used can help. The aim is comfortable daily life and wanted activities, not a particular hormone level or obligatory sexual schedule. If the plan is not helping, reconsider the diagnosis, product and need for specialist support rather than adding more remedies without review.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring a symptom timeline and every medicine, supplement and vaginal product to a clinician or pharmacist; describe any bleeding separately.

Choose purpose-made lubricant or moisturiser and ask whether a local prescription treatment fits your symptoms and medical history.

Agree on follow-up, stop activities or products that hurt, and seek urgent or emergency care for the warning signs described.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise symptom notes, product names and questions for your appointment. It cannot diagnose low oestrogen, infection or cancer, select a hormone product, assess bleeding safely or certify a supplement. App records should support a consultation and must not delay care.

When to seek help

Do not assume bleeding, changed discharge or persistent pain is simply dryness. Have any postmenopausal bleeding checked and contact pregnancy care immediately for bleeding while pregnant. Pelvic pain with fever, urinary symptoms, unusual discharge or possible pregnancy needs urgent advice. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, pain with movement or touch, shoulder-tip pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or loss of consciousness, or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency assessment. One-leg pain, redness or swelling needs urgent same-day advice; chest pain with breathlessness, stroke symptoms or tongue or throat swelling needs emergency help. Discuss hormonal products and cancer or clotting history with the prescriber; never push through painful sex.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Menopause-related oestrogen changes are common causes, but medicines, irritants and other conditions can also cause dryness.
  • Assessment should fit symptoms and medical history; cervical screening does not replace investigation of bleeding or infection symptoms.
  • Lubricant helps friction during activity, while a purpose-made moisturiser supports ongoing comfort.
  • Low-dose vaginal oestrogen has different absorption and risk considerations from systemic HRT; cancer history and other circumstances need individual advice.
  • Do not push through painful sex or dismiss bleeding as dryness; severe or worsening pain and other emergency signs need immediate help.

Frequently asked questions

What is the main hormonal cause of vaginal dryness?

Lower oestrogen can change the thickness, elasticity and comfort of vaginal tissues, particularly around menopause. It can also occur after birth, while breastfeeding or during some treatments. Dryness is not always hormonal, so the pattern and other symptoms matter.

Can medicines cause vaginal dryness?

Yes. Certain cold or allergy medicines, some antidepressants, hormonal contraception and cancer treatments can contribute. Show the exact medicines and timing to a clinician or pharmacist; do not stop essential treatment on your own.

When should I see a clinician?

Ask for help when dryness affects daily life or sex, persists, or simple measures have not helped after a few weeks. Unusual discharge, urinary symptoms or bleeding need assessment. Severe or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, loss of consciousness or breathing difficulty requires emergency help immediately.

What are the side effects of hormonal treatment?

They depend on product, route and medical history. Local treatment can cause headache, irritation, discomfort or spotting; other effects may occur. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen does not carry an identical risk profile to systemic HRT. Discuss unexplained bleeding, troublesome symptoms and personal cancer or clotting history with the prescriber.

Can I use a moisturiser only when having sex?

A vaginal moisturiser is generally used regularly according to its instructions for ongoing dryness. Lubricant is used around sexual activity for friction. Some people use both; choose products intended for the area and check condom compatibility.

Is vaginal oestrogen always forbidden after breast cancer?

An individual discussion is needed. Non-hormonal options are usually first, with specialist review of persistent symptoms and possible local oestrogen, particularly if taking an aromatase inhibitor. There is uncertainty about recurrence risk; do not self-prescribe.

Do I need regular intercourse to treat dryness?

No. Wanted arousal and comfortable stimulation may help lubrication, but there is no obligation to have penetration. Stop when it hurts and seek care for persistent discomfort. Avoiding painful sex does not mean you caused the tissue changes.

Are soy, black cohosh or wild yam safer cures?

They are not assured cures or automatically safer than prescribed treatment. Foods, extracts and research preparations differ, evidence has limitations and supplements can interact with medicines. Discuss the exact product rather than replacing assessment or a treatment plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
